newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ seen poised to act on monetary conditions.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ seen poised to act on monetary conditions.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is poised to act to curb a market-led easing of monetary conditions, economists said on Friday.
In the past 24 hours financial markets have taken conditions dangerously below the RBNZ's comfort zone, just weeks after similar levels were deemed too loose by the central bank.
"Certainly the market is testing the Reserve Bank's tolerance for easier monetary conditions," said Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank.
The market has failed to take short term interest rates high enough to offset a sharp decline in the New Zealand dollar's Trade-Weighted Index (TWI), which has caused conditions to ease.

The Monetary Conditions Index (MCI), which measures conditions using the RBNZ's stated trade-off between the currency's Trade-Weighted Index and 90-day bank bills, is now over 90 basis points equivalent below the bank's prefered line. "Last time they (the RBNZ) reacted in this sort of territory, so it wouldn't surprise me at all if they came out with something," said ANZ Treasurer Grant Spencer.

Economists said there were several factors which had presented the market with an opportunity to test the bank's resolve, foremost among them the expectation of an easing in the bank's impending Monetary Policy Statement on June 27.
"You always have this window of difficulty as you get closer to the Reserve Bank's next set of forecasts," Plank said.
"Does the Reserve Bank say anything because the market is inconsistent with its previous view? How much does it let its new view influence its comfort level?"
He said he believed the market had now eased conditions further than the bank was likely to allow in the MPS.
"But of course once the Reserve Bank sets a new level, that sets a new bottom of the range."
The market was in effect gambling that the bottom of the new range would probably be lower than where conditions were now.
"The problem is, at what point does the new bottom overtake the old bottom? The risk is that the market's being a bit premature," Plank said.
The RBNZ's announcement on Thursday that it would change the model it uses to assess monetary policy had also given markets an element of uncertainty to exploit, economists argued.

The bank said its new model would show how monetary conditions needed to evolve in order to achieve the desired inflation rate, making the potential implications for future monetary conditions more explicit.
Economists said some in the market had read more into the statement than was perhaps warranted.

"People are thinking, 'last time we had this easing bias that was implicit because of their inflation numbers, and we kind of had to guess how much easing was in there. Now they're going to be far more explicit, so maybe that gives us greater comfort to take conditions easier'," Plank said.
"It does add an element of uncertainty into the process."

There was also market talk that concerns over New Zealand's political stability and Treasury's recent downward revision of its 1997/98 growth forecasts had impacted on the currency, although economists gave less credence to that suggestion.
And they put to rest the idea that the bank would remain silent in the lead up to the MPS simply due to timing.
"I don't think they'd hold fire just because we're three weeks out from the MPS," said Spencer.
"I don't think they can afford to just leave it alone."
